examples.title: Filtering Rows
examples.description: Keep only the rows that match a condition
examples.markdown:
## Filtering rows

`pl.col('Flavor') == 'chocolate'` is an expression: polars works it out for every row at once, giving a column of True and False. `filter` keeps the rows where it is True.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

# Only the chocolate cones
chocolate = cones.filter(pl.col('Flavor') == 'chocolate')
chocolate

examples.title: Two Conditions
examples.markdown:
## Two conditions at once

`&` means both must be True, `|` means either. Each condition needs its own parentheses.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

# Cones over $4 that are not chocolate
pricey = cones.filter((pl.col('Price') > 4) & (pl.col('Flavor') != 'chocolate'))
pricey

examples.title: Sorting Rows
examples.description: Put rows in order of a column
examples.markdown:
## Sorting

`sort` puts the rows in order of a column. polars has no index, so a row's position is its only label.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

# Most expensive first
by_price = cones.sort('Price', descending=True)
by_price

examples.title: Group and Average
examples.description: One row per group, with its mean
examples.markdown:
## Grouping

`group_by` gathers the rows with the same flavor; `agg` says what to work out for each group. `maintain_order=True` keeps the groups in the order they first appear.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

# Average price of each flavor
avg = cones.group_by('Flavor', maintain_order=True).agg(pl.col('Price').mean())
avg

examples.title: Counting Rows
examples.description: How many rows each group has
examples.markdown:
## Counting

`len()` counts the rows in each group.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

# How many cones of each flavor
counts = cones.group_by('Flavor', maintain_order=True).len()
counts

examples.title: Several Aggregations
examples.markdown:
## Several results per group

`agg` takes as many expressions as you like. `alias` names the column each one makes.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

# Cheapest and priciest cone of each flavor
range_ = cones.group_by('Flavor', maintain_order=True).agg(
    pl.col('Price').min().alias('cheapest'),
    pl.col('Price').max().alias('priciest'),
)
range_

examples.title: Joining Tables
examples.description: Match rows of two tables on a key
examples.markdown:
## Joining

`join` matches each cone with the freezer row of the same flavor. An inner join keeps only flavors found in both.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

in_stock = cones.join(stock, on='Flavor')
in_stock

examples.title: Left Join
examples.description: Keep every row of the left table
examples.markdown:
## A left join

`how='left'` keeps every cone; flavors with nothing in the freezer get null for `Tubs`.

everything = cones.join(stock, on='Flavor', how='left')
everything

examples.title: Adding a Column
examples.description: Work out a new column from others
examples.markdown:
## A new column

`with_columns` works an expression out for the whole column at once. `alias` names it.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

# A 10% sale
sale = cones.with_columns((pl.col('Price') * 0.9).alias('Sale'))
sale

examples.title: Selecting Columns
examples.markdown:
## Choosing columns

`select` makes a table from the columns and expressions you list, and nothing else.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

# Flavor and the price in cents
cents = cones.select('Flavor', (pl.col('Price') * 100).round(0).alias('Cents'))
cents

examples.title: Pivot
examples.markdown:
## Pivot

Each flavor becomes a row and each color a column; each cell is the mean price of the cones that fall into it.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

grid = cones.pivot(on='Color', index='Flavor', values='Price', aggregate_function='mean')
grid

examples.title: A Lazy Query
examples.description: Build a plan, then collect() it
examples.markdown:
## Lazy queries

`lazy()` makes a LazyFrame: each method adds to a plan and nothing runs yet. `collect()` optimizes the plan and runs it. The steps show the table after each part of the plan.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

summary = (
    cones.lazy()
    .filter(pl.col('Price') > 4)
    .group_by('Flavor', maintain_order=True)
    .agg(pl.col('Price').max())
    .sort('Price')
    .collect()
)
summary

examples.title: Chaining Operations
examples.description: Filter, add a column and sort in one expression
examples.markdown:
## A chain

Each method works on the result of the one before. Step through to see the table after each one.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

deals = (
    cones.filter(pl.col('Price') > 4)
    .with_columns((pl.col('Price') * 0.9).alias('Sale'))
    .sort('Sale')
)
deals

examples.title: Rows by Position
examples.description: The first rows, or rows and columns by position
examples.markdown:
## Rows by position

polars has no index: a row's position, counting from 0, is how you pick it. `head(n)` keeps the first n rows, and `df[rows, cols]` takes rows by position and columns by name. As in a Python slice, `1:3` stops before position 3.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

# The first three rows
cones.head(3)

# Rows 1 and 2, two of the columns
cones[1:3, ['Flavor', 'Price']]

examples.title: Dropping and Renaming
examples.description: Leave a column out and rename another
examples.markdown:
## Dropping and renaming

`drop` leaves columns out and `rename` changes names with a dictionary from old to new. Neither changes a value or a row.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

menu = cones.drop('Color').rename({'Price': 'Price ($)'})
menu

examples.title: Missing Values
examples.markdown:
## Missing values

polars marks a missing value as `null`. `null_count()` counts them in each column, `drop_nulls()` drops every row that has one, and `fill_null(0)` puts 0 in place of each null in a column 0 fits; a null in a text column stays.
cells: import polars as pl
ratings.null_count()

# Only the rows with nothing missing
ratings.drop_nulls()

# No rating counts as 0 stars
ratings.fill_null(0)

examples.title: Removing Copies
examples.description: One row per flavor with unique
examples.markdown:
## Removing copies

`unique` keeps one of each set of rows that are the same. With `subset`, rows only need to match in those columns; `keep='first'` keeps the first of each, and `maintain_order=True` keeps the rows in their order.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

# One cone of each flavor
cones.unique(subset='Flavor', keep='first', maintain_order=True)

examples.title: Counting Values
examples.description: How often each value appears in a column
examples.markdown:
## Counting values

`cones['Flavor']` is one column, a Series. `value_counts()` counts how often each value appears, giving a table of values and counts; `sort=True` puts the most common first.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones
cones['Flavor'].value_counts(sort=True)

examples.title: First Row of Each Group
examples.description: Keep rows from every group without combining them
examples.markdown:
## First row of each group

`group_by(...).head(n)` keeps the first n rows of each group as they are, instead of combining each group into one row.
cells: import polars as pl

# An ice cream shop's menu
cones = pl.DataFrame({
    'Flavor': ['strawberry', 'chocolate', 'vanilla', 'chocolate', 'strawberry', 'mint'],
    'Color': ['pink', 'light brown', 'white', 'dark brown', 'pink', 'green'],
    'Price': [3.55, 4.75, 4.25, 5.25, 3.95, 4.50],
})
cones

# The first cone listed of each flavor
cones.group_by('Flavor', maintain_order=True).head(1)
